new.why: The most famous opening sentence in American literature; its imperative brevity and withheld identity are constitutive of the novel's entire relationship between narrator and reader.

new.passage_hint: Whenever I find myself growing grim about the mouth; whenever it is a damp, drizzly November in my soul; whenever I find myself involuntarily pausing before coffin warehouses, and bringing up the rear of every funeral I meet; and especially whenever my hypos get such an upper hand of me, that it requires a strong moral principle to prevent me from deliberately stepping into the street, and methodically knocking people's hats off—then, I account it high time to get to sea as soon as I can.
new.why: The anaphoric 'whenever' cascade is the first great prosodic set-piece of the novel and establishes Ishmael's ironic-melancholic register; it is both culturally famous and formally signature.

new.passage_hint: This is my substitute for pistol and ball. With a philosophical flourish Cato throws himself upon his sword; I quietly take to the ship.
new.why: A critically celebrated aphorism that announces Ishmael's mock-heroic self-deprecation and the novel's habit of deflating grand gestures with deadpan understatement.

new.passage_hint: Posted like silent sentinels all around the town, stand thousands upon thousands of mortal men fixed in ocean reveries. Some leaning against the spiles; some seated upon the pier-heads; some looking over the bulwarks of ships from China; some high aloft in the rigging, as if striving to get a still better seaward peep.
new.why: The anaphoric 'some … some … some' catalogue of water-gazers is a sustained prosodic signature mid-chapter that compression pressure will otherwise flatten into summary.

new.passage_hint: And still deeper the meaning of that story of Narcissus, who because he could not grasp the tormenting, mild image he saw in the fountain, plunged into it and was drowned. But that same image, we ourselves see in all rivers and oceans. It is the image of the ungraspable phantom of life; and this is the key to it all.
new.why: The Narcissus passage is the chapter's philosophical climax and has attracted sustained critical attention as the key to the novel's epistemological project; 'the ungraspable phantom of life' is thematically load-bearing.

new.passage_hint: I abominate all honorable respectable toils, trials, and tribulations of every kind whatsoever. It is quite as much as I can do to take care of myself, without taking care of ships, barques, brigs, schooners, and what not. And as for going as cook,—though I confess there is considerable glory in that, a cook being a sort of officer on ship-board—yet, somehow, I never fancied broiling fowls;—though once broiled, judiciously buttered, and judgmatically salted and peppered, there is no one who will speak more respectfully, not to say reverentially, of a broiled fowl than I will.
new.why: This comic digression on cooking is textually distinctive for its willful bathos and absurdist escalation—exactly the kind of middle-chapter voice passage that compression routinely destroys.

new.passage_hint: Who ain't a slave? Tell me that. Well, then, however the old sea-captains may order me about—however they may thump and punch me about, I have the satisfaction of knowing that it is all right; that everybody else is one way or other served in much the same way—either in a physical or metaphysical point of view, that is; and so the universal thump is passed round, and all hands should rub each other's shoulder-blades, and be content.
new.why: The 'universal thump' passage is a philosophically loaded ironic leveling of hierarchy that critics read as Ishmael's democratic stoicism; it is interpretively weight-bearing and must survive compression.

new.passage_hint: "_Grand Contested Election for the Presidency of the United States._ "WHALING VOYAGE BY ONE ISHMAEL. "BLOODY BATTLE IN AFFGHANISTAN."
new.why: The mock-playbill interpolation is formally unique in the chapter—a typographically distinct structural joke that positions the whaling voyage as cosmic farce alongside world-historical events.

new.passage_hint: the invisible police officer of the Fates, who has the constant surveillance of me, and secretly dogs me, and influences me in some unaccountable way—he can better answer than any one else. And, doubtless, my going on this whaling voyage, formed part of the grand programme of Providence that was drawn up a long time ago. It came in as a sort of brief interlude and solo between more extensive performances.
new.why: The Fates-as-stage-managers conceit introduces the novel's central ironic theology of predestination and free will, critically recognized as thematically foundational.

new.passage_hint: I am tormented with an everlasting itch for things remote. I love to sail forbidden seas, and land on barbarous coasts. Not ignoring what is good, I am quick to perceive a horror, and could still be social with it—would they let me—since it is but well to be on friendly terms with all the inmates of the place one lodges in.
new.why: This self-characterization is critically read as Ishmael's defining psychological statement—his affinity for the monstrous while retaining sociability—and anchors his role as witness rather than hero.

new.passage_hint: the great flood-gates of the wonder-world swung open, and in the wild conceits that swayed me to my purpose, two and two there floated into my inmost soul, endless processions of the whale, and, mid most of them all, one grand hooded phantom, like a snow hill in the air.
new.why: The closing image of the chapter—'one grand hooded phantom, like a snow hill in the air'—is the first indirect figure of Moby Dick and is widely anthologized as one of the novel's great closing cadences.

new.passage_hint: meditation and water are wedded for ever
new.why: A lapidary aphorism embedded in the mid-chapter philosophical excursus on water-magnetism; its compressed finality is characteristic of Ishmael's register and is easily cut under compression pressure.

notes_previous: This opening chapter is wall-to-wall signature material; at 900 words (0.63×) there is little room to cut, and what cutting is done must fall on the Saco/Niagara/Tennessee-poet/Persian-and-Greek catalog and the broiled-ibis Egyptian digression, not on the anaphoric openings, the Narcissus close, the 'Who ain't a slave?' passage, or the final hooded-phantom image. Preserve Ishmael's first-person ironic register intact — do not neutralize the mock-grandiose diction ('abominate,' 'judgmatically,' 'idolatrous dotings'). Keep the three-part 'I always go to sea as a sailor' structure legible even if individual examples are trimmed. The playbill typography should be preserved as a formal gesture. Do not modernize 'thee/thou' — none appear here, but keep 'ain't' in 'Who ain't a slave?' and archaisms like 'nigh,' 'yonder,' 'hither' where they set register.
notes_new: This is a signature chapter requiring the densest preservation effort in the opening movement. The drafter must retain all three anaphoric structures intact: the 'whenever' cascade, the 'some … some' water-gazer catalogue, and the 'Finally / Again / No' structural tripling of Ishmael's reasons for going as a simple sailor. The Narcissus paragraph must close intact — do not reduce it to a paraphrase. The mock-playbill must retain its typographical form. The cook-and-broiled-fowl digression is essential voice material despite being plot-irrelevant; preserve at least its pivot ('I abominate all honorable respectable toils') and the comic escalation. 'Who ain't a slave?' must survive as a direct-speech fragment — it seeds the democratic-egalitarian theme. The chapter's closing cadence ('one grand hooded phantom, like a snow hill in the air') must be preserved verbatim. At 900 words the drafter has roughly 60% of the original; the heaviest cuts should fall on the repeated water-magnetism examples in the middle (Prairies, Niagara, the Tennessee poet — these can be compressed to one illustrative example plus the Narcissus payoff). Do not modernize 'hypos,' 'judgmatically,' or 'hunks' — these are register markers, not obscurities.
